content.title: Running a Node Service Under systemd
content.text:
If you deploy a Node application to a plain Linux server, you need something to start it on boot, restart it when it crashes, and collect its logs. systemd already does all three, and it is installed on every mainstream distribution. This walkthrough takes a small Node HTTP service and turns it into a managed unit.

Start with the assumptions. The application lives in /opt/orderbridge, its entry point is /opt/orderbridge/server.js, and it reads configuration from environment variables such as PORT and DATABASE_URL. Node is installed at /usr/bin/node. You do not want it running as root, so create a dedicated system user first:

sudo useradd --system --home /opt/orderbridge --shell /usr/sbin/nologin orderbridge
sudo chown -R orderbridge:orderbridge /opt/orderbridge

Next, put the secrets somewhere the unit can read but ordinary users cannot. Create /etc/orderbridge.env with one KEY=value pair per line and no quotes or export keywords:

PORT=3000
NODE_ENV=production
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/orders

Then lock it down with sudo chmod 600 /etc/orderbridge.env and sudo chown root:root /etc/orderbridge.env. systemd reads the file as root before dropping privileges, so the service user does not need access to it.

Now write the unit. Create /etc/systemd/system/orderbridge.service with the following contents:

[Unit]
Description=OrderBridge Node service
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=orderbridge
Group=orderbridge
WorkingDirectory=/opt/orderbridge
EnvironmentFile=/etc/orderbridge.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/orderbridge/server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5
NoNewPrivileges=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

A few of those lines deserve explanation. Type=simple tells systemd the process in ExecStart is the service itself, which is right for Node because it does not fork into the background. Restart=on-failure restarts the process when it exits with a non-zero code or is killed by a signal, but not when it exits cleanly with status 0, so a deliberate shutdown stays down. RestartSec=5 adds a five-second pause between attempts so a crash loop does not peg the CPU, and the StartLimit settings stop systemd from trying more than five times in a minute; after that the unit enters a failed state you will see in status output. After=network-online.target delays startup until the network is actually up, which matters if the service connects to a database at boot.

One gotcha with EnvironmentFile: if the file is missing, the unit fails to start. Prefix the path with a dash, as in EnvironmentFile=-/etc/orderbridge.env, if you want a missing file to be ignored instead. For a production service the hard failure is usually what you want.

With the file in place, tell systemd to reread its configuration and start the service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now orderbridge.service

The enable step creates the symlink that starts the unit at boot, and --now starts it immediately as well. Check that it is running with sudo systemctl status orderbridge. You should see Active: active (running) along with the main PID and the last few log lines. If it says failed, the log will tell you why.

Everything your service writes to stdout and stderr goes to the journal. Follow it live with:

journalctl -u orderbridge -f

To see only the current boot use journalctl -u orderbridge -b, and to see the last hundred lines use journalctl -u orderbridge -n 100. Because the journal records the exit code and signal of each crash, a line like Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE followed by Scheduled restart job is the signature of Restart=on-failure doing its work.

When you change the unit file, run daemon-reload again before restarting, otherwise systemd keeps using the old definition. When you change only the environment file, a plain sudo systemctl restart orderbridge is enough, because the file is read fresh on every start.

Finally, verify the crash behaviour yourself before you rely on it. Find the PID with systemctl show -p MainPID orderbridge, kill it with sudo kill -9 that number, wait five seconds, and check status again. The service should be back with a new PID and the journal should show the restart. If it is not, the most common cause is a permissions problem on the working directory or a missing environment variable, both of which will be in the log.

notes: Competent, correct, concrete tutorial with a complete unit file and follow-up commands. A correct judge should rate it as genuinely useful for someone doing this task, while recognising it is standard practice rather than novel insight.
